title: The second and third ways
hookLine: causes and contingent things point to a first cause and a necessary being

cards: At a family dinner, an old couple tells their story again. She nearly didn't go to the dance that night. Rain, a sore throat, a cousin who talked her into it at the last minute.
Everyone laughs. Then a granddaughter goes quiet, doing the math. If Grandma had stayed home, I wouldn't be here.
A whole person, hanging on a cousin and the weather. Thomas Aquinas follows that thought further. Not only, why am I here?
But, why is there anything at all? Today's word: the second and third ways.

teach.b: The second way is a cousin of yesterday's. Yesterday was change; today is being made at all. Thomas finds in the world an order of causes.
A lamp shines because current reaches it. The current runs because something drives it. Nothing can cause itself, he says, because it would have to exist before itself, which is impossible.
And in an ordered line of causes, take away the first and you take away the rest: no first cause, no middle ones, no last one. But there are causes, here, working.
So there is a first cause, to which, Thomas says, everyone gives the name of God. The third way goes deeper, into the granddaughter's question.
Some things can be, and can also not be. Flowers. Mountains, slowly.
People. They come to be and pass away. They don't have to exist.
Then a bold step. If everything were like that, at some point there could have been nothing at all. And from nothing, nothing begins.
So there would be nothing now. But there is something. So not everything can be the borrowing kind.

Something must exist of itself, not lent its being by anything else, and giving being to the rest. This, Thomas says, all speak of as God. Readers argue over that bold middle step; we'll come back to it tomorrow.
Scripture says the giving part plainly.

teach.h: HE WHO GIVETH TO ALL LIFE, AND BREATH.
teach.b: In Acts, in the Douay-Rheims, Paul says God is "he who giveth to all life, and breath, and all things." Every borrowed thing, on this view, is borrowing from someone.

how: Catholic philosophy courses often read the second and third ways together, the arguments from causes and from contingent things, and discuss where the third way's reasoning is contested.

games.q: what does “the second and third ways” mean?
o: arguments from causes and from things that needn't exist
two pilgrim routes walked to the great churches
the second and third days of creation in Genesis

games.q: the second and third ways — tap the pairs.
p: things that can be and not be

s: Thomas says a thing can be the cause of itself
he says nothing can, because it would have to exist before itself.
the third way starts from things that come to be and pass away
flowers, mountains, people: things that can be and can also not be.
the necessary being of the third way borrows its existence from another
Thomas argues for something that exists of itself and gives being to the rest.

games.q: you're with Thomas. everything you can point to could fail to exist. what does he say follows?
o: then something must exist of itself, not borrowing its being.
then the world must have existed forever.
games.why: if everything were the borrowing kind, Thomas reasons, there could once have been nothing, and from nothing, nothing begins. so something exists of itself, and this all speak of as God.

practice: Choose one thing near you, a mug, a sparrow, your own hand on your knee, and say quietly: this didn't have to be. Let the surprise sink in for a few breaths, then take a second thing and a third, without hurrying toward an answer.
If you pray, thank God that anything is here at all; if you don't, just let the question stand.

wordCard.voice: The second and third ways. Thomas's arguments from causes and from things that can fail to be: nothing makes itself, so there's a first cause, and something that exists of itself.

orig.note: Latin: necessary of itself — what the third way argues for, a being that doesn't borrow its existence.

carryVoice: Your line: why anything at all. The granddaughter's question, as big as it gets. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3 (the second and third ways)
